destination.title: Police Are Allowed to Lie to You Until You Confess — Even If You're Innocent

short41: Police said his fingerprints were at the scene.
It was all invented and legal. So
An elderly neighbor was found dead nearby.
An officer told Barry his prints were there.
The victim was a type-A secretor;
The swab carried only A-type material
the Supreme Court ruled in Frazier v.
Cupp that a lie about the evidence standing alone
does not make an otherwise voluntary confession inadmissible
it's the totality of the circumstances.
DNA cleared Barry sixteen years later. For adults
Follow for the cases they don't teach you.

candidate_payload_lines: Florida's Supreme Court declined review in 1990 and never ruled on the merits.

"The fact that the police misrepresented the statements that Rawls had made is, while relevant, insufficient in our view to make this otherwise voluntary confession inadmissible." The Court did not bless the lie.
Officers testified that nobody had told him about it.
On the morning of August 13, 1987, a neighbor saw Edna Laughman out in her yard.
In 1987, before DNA typing, that was the strongest exclusion science could offer.
Officers testified that they had never given those details to Barry, or to his family.
On December 16, 1988, Barry Laughman was convicted of murder, rape, robbery and burglary, and sentenced to life.
Once Miranda swallowed the rest, what survived from 1969 is narrow.
In November 2003 the laboratory Orchid Cellmark ran Y-STR testing on the same evidence, and the result excluded Barry Laughman.
In August 2004 a new trial was granted, and on August 26, 2004, the Adams County District Attorney, Shawn C.
Then, in August 2018, the same vaginal swab that had cleared him was sent to a private laboratory, Parabon NanoLabs, for genetic genealogy.
On July 14, 2021, Adams County District Attorney Brian Sinnett announced that Christopher Speelman's DNA was, in his words, an absolute match to the crime scene evidence.
On June 22, 2023, Chris Joseph Larry Speelman, then fifty-nine, pleaded guilty to third-degree murder and burglary and no contest to rape.
Judge Thomas Campbell sentenced him to twenty-five to fifty years, with no parole eligibility until 2046.
He died on March 21, 2024, at Jefferson Einstein Hospital in Philadelphia, at sixty.
He had twenty years of freedom, and almost none of them are in the record this film is built from.
Of the 257 cases the Innocence Project has won, the average client served sixteen years.
Lay those 257 sentences end to end and they come to four thousand, one hundred and two years.

shorts.angle: Officers may speak a lie about the evidence, and one Florida court held they may not print that lie on a letterhead.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What a spoken lie about a fingerprint took from a man with the comprehension of a ten-year-old.
shorts.loop_join: L5 stops on the part left wide open, and L1 completes the clause: police are allowed to lie to your face about the evidence.

lines.text: Police are allowed to lie to your face about the evidence. There is one thing a court has said they cannot do. Put the lie on paper.
source_lines: For adults, no state has a law that generally forbids an officer from lying to your face about the evidence.

lines.text: Florida, 1989. Officers manufactured two fake scientific reports, one on a state agency's letterhead, one on a private company's, and showed them to a suspect.
source_lines: In State v. Cayward, decided by Florida's Second District Court of Appeal on November 15, 1989, officers manufactured two fake scientific reports — one on the letterhead of the Florida Department of Criminal Law Enforcement, one on the letterhead of a company called Life Codes, Inc.

lines.text: The court upheld the suppression of his confession. Spoken deception, it said, is one thing. Fabricated documents that impersonate a real institution have no place in the criminal justice system.
source_lines: The court upheld the suppression of his confession. Spoken deception, it said, is one thing; fabricated documents that impersonate a real institution have no place in the criminal justice system.

lines.text: So the line is not the lie. It is the letterhead. They may say it. In some courts, they may not print it.
source_lines: They may say it. In some courts, they may not print it.

shorts.angle: Roughly ten states now bar police from lying to a child in an interrogation, and not one bars it for you.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What that lie did to a twenty-four-year-old the law counted as an adult.
shorts.loop_join: L5 says nothing but the law made him an adult, so L1's finding about lying to a child lands on the restart as a statement about him.

lines.text: A lie with a badge behind it roughly triples the odds that a child will confess to something they did not do.
source_lines: A lie with a badge behind it roughly triples the odds that a child will confess to something they did not do.

lines.text: Among people later exonerated, thirty-four percent of those convicted as children had falsely confessed, against ten percent of those convicted as adults.
source_lines: Among exonerees convicted as children, 34 percent had falsely confessed, against 10 percent of those convicted as adults.

lines.text: So legislatures started with the children. Oregon and Illinois signed laws a day apart in July 2021. Both took effect on January 1st, 2022, and by 2026 roughly ten states have some version of it.

lines.text: The man in this story was twenty-four, with an IQ of seventy. The law counted him as an adult. Nothing else about him did.
